fixes.explanation: Yes, guarding his mouth. “He who guards his mouth protects his life, but the one who opens his lips invites his own ruin.” Solomon sets two men side by side. One guards his mouth and protects his life, and the other opens his lips and invites his own ruin. Keep that mouth on a short leash, friend.

Yes, advice. “Arrogance leads only to strife, but wisdom is with the well-advised.” Solomon says wisdom is with the well-advised, the people who take advice. Arrogance, on the other hand, leads only to strife.

That's it. “Dishonest wealth will dwindle, but what is earned through hard work will be multiplied.” Dishonest wealth is the one that dwindles. What is earned through hard work is the part that gets multiplied.

Yes, righteous. “A good man leaves an inheritance to his children’s children, but the sinner’s wealth is passed to the righteous.” The sinner's wealth is passed to the righteous, and that's the whole answer. Not the owner's plan, I bet.
Yes. “Abundant food is in the fallow ground of the poor, but without justice it is swept away.” The food was there, and it still got swept away. Solomon names the cause plainly: without justice.

Right, that one is false. Solomon says, “A righteous man eats to his heart’s content, but the stomach of the wicked is empty.” The stomach of the wicked is empty, not full. The righteous man is the one who eats to his heart's content.

Solomon, David's son and Israel's king (Proverbs 1:1), says it plainly: “…a mocker does not listen to rebuke.” The mocker is the one who does not listen. Set beside him is the wise son who heeds his father's discipline.

No stranger walks into this verse, friend. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king (Proverbs 1:1), names the mocker as the one who does not listen to rebuke. The other side of the matchup is the wise son, who heeds his father's discipline.

Right, baker. The verse says the desire of the faithless is violence, and peace isn't in it. Across from that, a man enjoys good things from the fruit of his lips. Solomon sets the two statements side by side.
Restless is a fair guess, but it isn't the word in this verse. Solomon says the slacker craves yet has nothing, and the soul of the diligent is fully satisfied. The diligent end up satisfied.

Yes. “Righteousness guards the man of integrity, but wickedness undermines the sinner.” Righteousness does the guarding, and wickedness does the undermining. Picture a cookie box with the bottom already gone.
I'd love a little applause too, but this verse isn't handing any out. Solomon says riches may ransom a man's life, but a poor man hears no threat. That's the word you're after, baker.
Double is a fair guess, but Solomon uses a different word. He says what is earned through hard work will be multiplied. Dishonest wealth goes the other direction and dwindles.

True. Verse 12 says, “Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but desire fulfilled is a tree of life.” Solomon names both the sick heart and the tree of life. The second half is the one this card asked about.
Yes. The teaching of the wise is “…a fountain of life, turning one from the snares of death.” A snare is a trap. The teaching turns a person away from it.
Yes. A wicked messenger falls into trouble, but a faithful envoy brings healing. Solomon puts the two messengers side by side. The faithful one brings healing, and that's a good job to have.
Late messengers are a pain, I'll grant you, but delay isn't in this verse. Solomon says a faithful envoy brings healing. The wicked messenger is the one who falls into trouble.
Not quite. Solomon says a righteous man eats to his heart's content, but the stomach of the wicked is empty. Empty, not full. That's the part this card flipped.
